title: Guha the boatman
hook: two men keep watch by a fire all night, and in the morning a charioteer is sent home

segments.voice: Yesterday: Guha the boatman, king of the Nishadas, Rama's friend as dear as his own life. Did you reach out to a friend? Today, the night watch on the riverbank. Day five hundred thirty-five.

Some of the most honest conversations happen late at night, beside someone who isn't family, when the people you love are asleep a few feet away. Rama and Sita are lying on a bed of grass under a tree. The fire is low. Lakshmana is sitting up with his bow across his knees. Guha comes and sits beside him. They barely know each other. By morning, they'll have shared something neither of them will forget.
screen: `LATE NIGHT, BY A FIRE.` → `TWO MEN WHO BARELY KNOW EACH OTHER.`

segments.voice: Guha speaks first, kindly. I've made a comfortable bed for you, he tells Lakshmana. Go and sleep. My people and I will keep watch. We know this forest. Nothing will happen to Rama while we're here. Lakshmana says no. How can I sleep, he asks, when my brother, who should be lying in a palace, is lying on the ground? And then he starts to say out loud what he's been carrying all day. He talks about the old king, whom he thinks won't survive the grief. About Kausalya and Sumitra, who will be alone in the palace. About the city, emptied of joy. Guha listens, and Valmiki says Guha weeps too, as the night goes on. Two strangers, one grief. In the morning, Rama asks Guha for the milky sap of a banyan tree. With it, he and Lakshmana mat their hair into the coils that forest ascetics wear. It's the moment their old life visibly ends. Then Rama turns to Sumantra, the charioteer who has driven them all this way. Go back now, he says. Comfort my father. Tell him we're well. Sumantra begs to stay. Let me come with you, he says. How can I drive an empty chariot into Ayodhya? The people will think I've abandoned you. Rama answers with care. You must go back, he says, so that Kaikeyi believes I've truly left, and stops doubting my father. Sumantra turns the horses for home. Now the only ones left are Rama, Sita, Lakshmana, and a friend with a boat.
screen: `GO AND SLEEP. I'LL KEEP WATCH.` · `HOW CAN I SLEEP?` · `TWO STRANGERS, ONE GRIEF.` · `MATTED HAIR AT DAWN.` · then, large: `SUMANTRA TURNS FOR HOME.`

segments.voice: Sit as if beside a low fire at night. Let the breath be quiet. Think of a worry you carry for someone else, a parent, a child, a friend, that you haven't said out loud. Let yourself say it silently now, in a few plain words, as Lakshmana did to Guha. Then just keep watch with it, breathing, the way two people keep watch by a fire. The bell holds the time.
Guha the boatman, part two. He keeps watch all night beside Lakshmana and weeps with him, and at dawn Rama sends the charioteer home.
Your line: Guha the boatman. Today, if someone tells you what they're carrying, just listen, and stay. Day five hundred thirty-five.

howItsDone: Matted hair, jata, is still worn by many Hindu ascetics as a sign of renunciation; in the text Rama and Lakshmana mat their hair with banyan sap on the Ganga's bank.

fork.setup: you're Rama. your loyal charioteer begs to follow you into exile. what do you tell him?
options: go back, so Kaikeyi believes I've truly left.
fork.reveal: Rama sends him home to comfort the king and to show Kaikeyi that Rama has really gone.

original.note: Sanskrit jaṭā: matted hair, the coils worn by forest ascetics; Rama and Lakshmana take it on at the Ganga.

trapdoor: what you thought: Guha only ferries Rama across the river.
what it means: he keeps watch all night and shares Lakshmana's grief.
what a scholar hears: Valmiki gives the night conversation to Guha and Lakshmana, not to Rama, so the grief of the household is voiced by a brother and a friend.
